findings.title: Permission denial cache can mask newly granted permissions for up to the full TTL
findings.body: In Check(), the permDenialCache lookup happens unconditionally before any attempt to re-check real permissions. Once a (user, action, name, parent) combination is cached as denied (line 154, s.permDenialCache.Set), subsequent Check calls return Allowed=false immediately for shortCacheTTL (30s) regardless of whether the user's permissions have since been updated (e.g. an admin granted access, or a role change). Unlike the main permCache fallback added in this PR for Check (which re-queries the DB when the cached permission map doesn't contain the resource), there is no equivalent re-validation path for the denial cache - a hit always short-circuits to deny without consulting the DB. This means that after a legitimate denial, a user who is subsequently granted access can still be denied access for up to 30 seconds, which is a new correctness/UX regression introduced by this feature; there is no cache invalidation hook tied to permission changes.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels cache-hit-but-insufficient results as cache misses
findings.body: When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (cache hit, err == nil) but checkPermission determines the cached map does not grant access for the specific resource, execution falls through past the if-block to line 137, which unconditionally records permissionCacheUsage with label "false" (cache miss). This mislabels a scenario where the cache was actually hit (just insufficient for this specific resource) as a full cache miss, understating the real cache hit rate in metrics/dashboards used to monitor cache effectiveness.

findings.title: List() does not get the same stale-cache fallback that Check() received, so newly created resources may still be missing from list results
findings.body: The PR's stated goal is to let dashboard/folder creators immediately access resources they just created. Check() was updated to fall back to a fresh DB query when the cached permission map does not satisfy the specific resource being checked (lines 123-137). List(), however, only distinguishes cache-hit vs cache-miss at the whole-permission-map level (lines 180-192): if getCachedIdentityPermissions returns any cached map at all, it is used as-is with no verification that it contains a newly created resource. As a result, a user who just created a dashboard/folder may be able to Check access to it directly, but it can still be absent from List() results (e.g. for a folder/dashboard browser) until the permission cache naturally expires (shortCacheTTL, 30s). This is an incomplete fix relative to the PR's described motivation and is not covered by any new test.

findings.title: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates variable-length fields with a non-unique delimiter, risking key collisions
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the cache key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent, using plain underscore concatenation. Because userUID, name, and parent are externally supplied identifiers (resource UIDs, folder UIDs) that are not guaranteed to be free of underscores, two different (action, name, parent) combinations could produce the identical concatenated string (e.g. action="a_b", name="c" vs action="a", name="b_c"), causing an unrelated resource's permission check to incorrectly hit another resource's cached denial entry. This would surface as a user being denied access to a resource they actually have permission to, due to an unrelated cached denial colliding on the same key.
